high:
I am an anonymous adult with ordinary relationships and activities. A confident or forceful person can intimidate me, and I may find it difficult to stand up for myself even when I know my own position. I can want to answer while feeling unable to get my defense into the conversation.

I am easily embarrassed by small social slips. In a group whose customs are unclear, I may fear doing the wrong thing and feel exposed by a harmless correction. This concern can arise without anyone insulting me or anything serious having gone wrong.

Approaching people can be difficult even when I would like their company. I tend to feel truly comfortable with friends and less at ease before familiarity develops. Attention can also frighten me: being asked to speak briefly may feel exposing, and I can stumble over words I know how to say.

Unfamiliar settings and difficult social moments often leave me awkward and self-conscious. A strained conversation can bother me even when I understand the practical issue. These tendencies have ordinary exceptions; I may enjoy people, value discussion, have useful ideas, and act confidently in a familiar activity. My interest in company, kindness, competence and leadership preferences vary independently. No clinical label, constant avoidance, or lack of speech ability is implied.
low:
I am an anonymous adult with ordinary relationships and activities. Another person's confidence usually does not intimidate me, and I can stand up for myself when an everyday situation calls for it. I can state my position without needing to dominate the whole conversation or win every disagreement.

Small social slips rarely embarrass me much. I can join an ordinary group activity without being preoccupied by fear of doing the wrong thing, and a harmless correction usually feels manageable. This does not mean that I never regret a mistake or ignore how others feel.

I can generally approach someone new without strong awkwardness. My comfort is not restricted to established friends, although I may still prefer some people or settings. Drawing attention to myself for a routine purpose is usually unfrightening, and my words ordinarily come out without much stumbling.

I tend to feel comfortable in unfamiliar settings and remain fairly unbothered by difficult social moments. A strained exchange can be inconvenient without making me feel exposed. These tendencies have ordinary exceptions; I may want quiet, decline company, lack an answer, or avoid leading a group. My interest in company, kindness, competence and leadership preferences vary independently. No constant sociability, perfect eloquence, or immunity to every embarrassment is implied.
